# 19-veles — sources

Back-test entry `19-veles.yaml`: Veles, a pricing copilot for enterprise sales teams (YC Winter 2024, W24).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's choice"
marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC post of
2024-02-23 and the months around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era where one exists;
anything later is marked as later, and a later price sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Veles - Your copilot for enterprise sales", 2024-02-23 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/KTD-veles-your-copilot-for-enterprise-sales
- [HOME24] getveles.com as archived 2024-04-19 (home page with customer quotes) — https://web.archive.org/web/20240419015813/https://www.getveles.com/
- [PRICE24] getveles.com/pricing as archived 2024-05-25, the first archived snapshot of the pricing page (the next, 2024-06-17, is identical) — https://web.archive.org/web/20240525193905/https://www.getveles.com/pricing
- [PRICE] getveles.com/pricing today, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.getveles.com/pricing
- [YCP] YC company page today, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/veles
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, wholesale and manufacturing sales representatives, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/sales/wholesale-and-manufacturing-sales-representatives.htm

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Account executives who price and quote enterprise software deals; their sales leadership.
   [LYC] "equip your sales team with an AI-powered quoting tool ... give reps a tool they will actually love, and
   leadership the actionable insights they need to move the needle." [LYC] "we're on a mission to make every rep a top
   performer." → `roles[rep]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "selling software to enterprises" (the
   post's "SaaS Pricing Calculator" and "enterprise sales deals").

2. **What (the job).** Price each enterprise deal accurately and on standard terms.
   [LYC] "Pricing enterprise sales deals is a headache. Fragmented processes and tools result in subpar terms and lost
   opportunities." [LYC] the solution ensures "accurate pricing and standard terms". → `statements.problem`,
   `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** When a buyer asks for a quote and the pricing has to be worked out and approved.
   [LYC] "Many teams resort to complex Google Sheets, Slides/PPTs, manual CRM entries, and email chains just to handle
   pricing." [LYC] the tool helps reps "navigate the quoting and negotiation process effectively". [HOME24] (a customer)
   "Veles gives us those insights while optimizing a daily activity for salespeople and saving them time."
   → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: deal quote`. Author's choice: the window {4, WEEKS} (a weekly rhythm, the
   diversity research's reading; spec 120's WEEKS) and Frequency 2 to 4 weeks out of 4. Prevalence `p_80_100`: an
   account executive on an enterprise team quotes at least once in four weeks.

4. **Which people.** Sales teams of up to ten at US software companies selling enterprise deals.
   [PRICE24] both paid plans are "Up to 10 team members". [LYC] "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ, and BI
   platforms". → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (the team and the testimonials are US; no other
   market is named).

5. **Who pays.** The sales team's budget; the sales director chooses; finance agrees to the discount rules.
   [LYC] "Leadership lacks scalable insight into sales negotiations, hindering optimization and guidance for sales
   reps." [HOME24] the quoted customers are a "Founder & CEO", a "President & Cofounder" and a "VP of Business
   Development". → `persona.decision_maker: {role: director}`, Buyer and payer tests "The CFO" (a RevOps lead listed).
   Author's choice: no source names the buyer's title or who must agree; the CFO is the author's reading of "deal desk
   rules" and "minimize discounting" (discount policy is finance's). Purchase friction's three items (a CRM check —
   tested; agreeing the discount rules with finance; a security review) are the author's, the first from [LYC]
   "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ, and BI platforms" and [PRICE24] "Pre-built Integrations" on Growth.
   Commitment's step, "try it on one sales team's deals": [LYC] "Book a demo with us here"; the trial is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** One calculator with the price book, the deal desk rules and peer benchmarks; leadership sees every
   deal's pricing.
   [LYC] "Veles offers an easy-to-use calculator, benchmarks for comparing deals against those of peers, and clear
   guidance on deal desk rules, ensuring accurate pricing and standard terms." [LYC] "SaaS Pricing Calculator: Easily
   standardize pricing and track sales rep behavior in one intuitive platform." [LYC] "designed to enhance negotiation
   skills, minimize discounting, and land larger deals with confidence." [HOME24] "Track how sales reps are
   negotiating, discounting, offering concessions, and presenting pricing to your customers."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (the deal already in the CRM — tested; a written price
   book; one tool) and Adoption friction (every quote in the calculator, not spreadsheets — tested; record each
   concession). Relative advantage's two benefits: [HOME24] (a customer) "a well engineered pricing calculator provided
   reps to close deals faster" (shorter_time) and [LYC] "minimize discounting" (fewer_attempts, fewer rounds of
   discount); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** $250 to $500 per sales team a month; the cost is deals lost or signed on worse terms.
   [PRICE24] "Startup ... $250.00 USD /month ... Up to 10 team members"; "Growth ... $500.00 USD /month ... Pre-built
   Integrations ... Up to 10 team members"; "Enterprise ... Contact Sales". → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $250 to
   $500 per sales team (the cost's unit and month).
   Existing sacrifice, RATE 2 to 4 deals of the deals they quote per sales team a month, lossPhrase "Deals lost or
   signed on worse terms because the pricing was worked out by hand": author's reading of [LYC] "subpar terms and lost
   opportunities"; no source gives a count or a percent. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a count of
   deals never compares with dollars). `hourly_rate` 50 (the loader wants one on a B2B entry; the chain does not read
   it): [BLS] "$104,920 in May 2025" for technical and scientific products, about $50 an hour.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [LYC] "Slow Ramp: Onboarding new sales reps takes 5 - 7 months due to poorly documented pricing strategies and
   variations across companies." [LYC] "No Knowledge Share: Top performers' insights are trapped, preventing learning
   and team-wide improvement." [HOME24] "There is also a lot of information that is lost in the front end of the
   negotiation." [YCP] (today, a later framing used only for one story) "You closed your first few deals on handshakes
   and Stripe links. Now a customer wants a ramp-up, custom terms, or annual billing — and suddenly you're duct-taping
   spreadsheets to your CRM."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Account executives (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Jordan Okafor → [LYC] "Google Sheets, Slides/PPTs, manual CRM entries, and email chains"; the ramp and the two-day approval wait are the author's.
- Priyanka Raghunathan → [LYC] the slow ramp and "poorly documented pricing strategies"; a new rep asking three people.
- Mateo Fernández → author's invention, filling a gap: a rep whose CPQ already holds the price book, so the problem is not a chorus; against on Importance.
- Aisha Bello → [LYC] "minimize discounting"; [HOME24] "information that is lost in the front end of the negotiation": a discount given without knowing what similar deals closed at.
- Connor Walsh → author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped (rather_not_say) story, GUESSED by code.
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, habitual story with no one occasion (GUESSED).
- Tobias Becker → author's invention: a gate No (on leave in the window).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → author's invention: a gate No (only renewals, quoted by another team, in the window).
- Darnell Hayes → [YCP]'s later "handshakes and Stripe links" framing: a small seller whose deals are not in a CRM, so the tested condition fails (Compatibility only with help).
- Ingrid Halvorsen → [LYC] "Top performers' insights are trapped": a top performer who trusts her own sheet (Current solution mostly works; Relative advantage negative).
- Rahul Menon → [LYC] "email chains"; the deal desk approval and three versions of one quote are the author's.
- Sofia Marchetti → [HOME24] "Track how sales reps are negotiating, discounting, offering concessions": logging every concession is more admin (Adoption friction probably not).

Sales directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Grant Whitaker, Tanya Brooks → [HOME24] the customers' praise ("gives us insights we haven't had before"): pay within the plans, the CFO agrees.
- Kwabena Asante → [PRICE24] "Enterprise ... Contact Sales": a larger team that would pay above $500 (beyond the founder's band).
- Lucia Moreno, Elena Petrova → [LYC] "Book a demo"; [LYC] "Integrated seamlessly with your CRM, CPQ": would start only after a demo or a live-deal trial.
- Heather Lindqvist → author's invention: a small team that would pay under $250 until it is proven.
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention, filling a gap: a team whose CPQ already quotes; Nothing as the cost, would not pay.
- Victor Nakamura → author's invention: the price set against what the CRM costs; someone else agreed.

The share at or above $250 (5 of 8) is the author's: no public account gives Veles's conversion at launch; the
customer quotes on [HOME24] are vendor-curated. No respondent carries the name of a customer, commenter or founder.

## Status today

Widened. [YCP] now reads "CPQ for humans and agents" and addresses early-stage founders ("Veles is built for you. AI
agents handle quoting, approvals, and deal docs end-to-end so you can run a real sales motion without hiring a deal
desk."). Price today, [PRICE]: "Pay per active contract, not per seat"; "$ 8 / contract / mo First 10 contracts free.
Unlimited seats. No credit card required to start."; Enterprise "Custom". The launch-era per-team plans ($250 and $500 a
month) are gone.

## Could not be sourced

- **The cost.** The launch post names the loss ("subpar terms and lost opportunities") but no number; the 2 to 4 deals
  per sales team a month is the author's reading in the founder's terms, chosen as a count a sales director can recall.
- **The price at launch itself.** The first archived pricing page is three months after the Launch YC post; it is
  used as the launch-era price (no earlier price is public).
- **The buyer's title and who must agree.** No source names them; "Sales directors" and "The CFO" are the author's.
- **A launch-era rate of how often a rep quotes.** The weekly rhythm is the diversity research's reading; [LYC] says
  only that pricing is handled per deal.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person rep accounts.** None exists; the occasions are scripted from [LYC], [HOME24]
  (vendor-curated quotes) and one later framing from [YCP].
- The launch post's quota line ("On average 60% of sales reps hit quota due to fragmented tooling") reads as if
  "miss" was meant; it is not used as a figure.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction items, the Purchase friction items but the CRM check, and every pick are the
  author's.

screens.why2: "Quote", "calculator", "spreadsheets" and "concession" are everyday words on an enterprise sales floor, though the intro repeats the title word for word.
screens.why3: These are exactly what my reps would have to change in their own deals: quoting in our tool instead of their Google Sheets, and logging concessions as they negotiate.
screens.why4: The two steps are distinct and are the real asks of a rep; the one I'd test first, quoting in the calculator, is the belief drafted.
screens.why5: Both rows are my launch words, every quote in the calculator and tracking each concession, kept as I meant them.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the two efforts Keel wrote from my adoption answer, it makes sense to pick the one strangers will be tested on, matching how the compatibility step worked.
screens.why2: "Build every quote in the calculator, not spreadsheets" and "record each concession" are exactly how I talk about my reps' workflow, and "the effort most likely to stop them" reads cleanly on first pass.
screens.why3: I know from every demo that getting reps off their Google Sheets is the real hurdle, so I can answer this without guessing.
screens.why4: Both options are my own two adoption items, distinct from each other, and nothing I typed is missing.
screens.why5: The belief and test, "Most would build every quote in the calculator, not spreadsheets," say exactly what I meant, with no rewording.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the obvious moment to decide whether to collect emails from reps and directors who want to try it, and I book demos anyway.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is everyday B2B sales language to me, and the hint spells out exactly what respondents will see and where I will find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want a list of teams willing to try the calculator on live deals is my own call as founder.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the whole choice, the two options are distinct, and nothing is missing.
screens.why5: Nothing of Veles's name or roles leaks into the end line, and it matches my step of trying it on one sales team's deals.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the account executives, it is obvious I next pick how they answer, just before sending; only the kicker 'INTERVIEWS · SENT' reads oddly, since nothing has been sent yet.
screens.why2: The choice is clear, but the doubled 'Daphne Daphne' and the status lines 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes' and 'Ready when Daphne is' need a second read to work out that the AI option is not ready yet.
screens.why3: I know my reps: they are busy, live in the CRM and their phones, and would rather tap through between calls than talk to a video, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: AI voice, read-and-tap, and let them choose cover the real choices, are distinct, and need no escape option.
screens.why5: It keeps 'account executives' as I typed it and shows nothing of Veles to the respondent.
screens.instead: How should account executives answer? — Read and tap (ready now) / Talk to Daphne, an AI interviewer (ready in a few minutes) / Let them pick when they open the link

screens.why1: After choosing who asks and how account executives answer, deciding who receives the interview links is the natural last step before sending.
screens.why2: The three choices are worded plainly, and each says how its link is made and sent, so I can pick on first reading.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm sending to AEs I know by name, to a list I pulled, or posting in a community where sales reps already gather.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I'd reach reps, but there is no escape or 'not sure yet' chip, and 'the Contacts page' is a Keel term I haven't seen in this flow.
screens.why5: My pick, people I know by name, is kept as typed, and nothing of Veles or the sales-director role leaks into the respondent's side.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (one link each) / A list I find with Keel (one link each) / One open link I post where account executives gather / Not sure yet

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits under the title, and each card gives the deciding number beside it, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know nothing was called and that one answer per belief was missing.
screens.why_b2: The tally '3 too few · 7 people answered' is plain, but it sits beside cards that each say 4 answered, so I had to look twice to work out why only 4 of my 7 count and where the other 3 went.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry exactly the three belief lines I checked on the way in, word for word.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need more answers, but the screen never says to get one more rep per belief or why three people's answers did not count, so the next step is left for me to infer.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the data: every card says too few and shows 4 of the 5 needed, and nothing is called held or not held.
screens.instead: Too few to call on all three beliefs: only 4 of your 7 reps could answer each (3 had no quote in the window); get at least one more account executive who quoted in the last 4 weeks to call them.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside its deciding number, "4 counted, 5 needed", so I know there's no call and why.
screens.why_b2: The bars and the four-plus-one-ghost strip show 3 yes, 1 with steps and 0 no over 4, but a bar written as "3 of 4" next to a "no more than 1 in 3 say no" rule took me a second look to square.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and "the deal was already set up in the CRM" are exactly the belief I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic: it doesn't tell me that one more counted answer would decide it, or that all four counted lean my way.
screens.why_b5: The lean-not-a-call wording keeps it honest, but the header says "4 answered" while the count line says "5 answered · 4 counted", which misstates who answered.
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 counted say the deal was in the CRM (Mei-Ling's guess not counted); one more counted answer would decide it, so send the study to a few more account executives.

screens.why_b1: The verdict, Too few to call, sits right beside the number that decides it: 4 counted against the 5 needed, and the So line repeats that tie.
screens.why_b2: It is plain that the chart counts better against same over the 4 counted. But the doubled figures ('Better · 3 3 a lot · 0 a little') and a bar written as '3 of 4' next to '1 of 4 said no difference or worse' make me look twice to see that 3 for is right at my bar.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage and 'the quote built and approved the same day' are word for word the belief I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it does not tell me that 3 of 4 already lean my way and that one more counted rep, describing a real recent quote, decides it.
screens.why_b5: The headline says '4 answered · 5 needed' while the count line says 5 answered, so it reads as if five people were in and it still was not called; the header should say 4 counted, although the verdict itself does not overclaim.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 5 answers counted (Mei-Ling's was a guess); 3 of 4 say a lot better, which is at your bar, so one more rep who tells you about a real recent quote settles it.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits beside "4 answered · 5 needed", but the count line says "5 answered · 4 counted", so the verdict's own number misnames counted as answered and I have to reconcile the two.
screens.why_b2: The bars for Yes, Yes-if-worth-it, Probably not and No are plain and the strip shows 3 for, 1 against and 1 ghost, but "your bar · 3 of 4" reads like my result rather than the threshold, so it takes a second look to see where the bar sits.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and "Most would build every quote in the calculator, not spreadsheets" are exactly the belief I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic: it doesn't say that 3 of 4 lean my way or that one more countable answer would settle it.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the low n is said outright ("a small group: a lean, not a call"), Mei-Ling's guess is set aside, and nothing is called held.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 5 answered, 4 counted (Mei-Ling's was a guess), 5 needed. 3 of 4 would build every quote in Veles, one only if clearly worth it, so it leans held; get one more clear answer to settle it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no answer yet and exactly why.
screens.why_b3: 'Relative advantage' and 'the quote built and approved the same day' are the dimension and belief I checked on the way in, word for word.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' tells me to get one more answer, but nothing says what the lone 'no difference' means for the idea, such as whether teams that already run a CPQ are the wrong segment.
screens.why_b5: The count line '1 against · 1 asked their why here' and '4 answered' keep the tiny n in view, and the screen claims no verdict, so nothing overreaches.
screens.why_b6: Mateo's quote adds something I never typed: on a team whose price book already lives in a CPQ, quoting takes minutes and the week goes to pipeline and forecast, so my pain may only exist where pricing lives in sheets.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 answered, 1 more needed; the one 'no difference' came from a rep whose CPQ already holds the price book, so ask whether your targets quote from sheets or from a CPQ.

screens.why1: Opening on whether a quote of mine got stuck in pricing approval lately is the obvious place to start, and it sets up the story question that follows.
screens.why2: Quotes and pricing approval are my everyday words, and I can answer this on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether a deal of mine sat waiting on deal desk or my VP's sign-off this month.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but a gate should carry no escape; 'I can't recall one particular quote' doesn't answer 'did any', and 'I'd rather not say' is a second, banned chip.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's quote-approval wait without leaking any product or their terms for people like me.
screens.why6: One short question and 'Yes or no' is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: In the last 4 weeks, did any of your quotes get held up in pricing approval? Yes · No (no escape chips)

screens.why1: Right after asking whether my quotes got stuck in pricing approval, showing me an idea for building and approving quotes is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: CRM, CPQ, deal desk, standard terms and discounting are words I use every day, so I take this in on one read.
screens.why3: Building a quote, working the deal desk rules and getting leadership to sign off on pricing is exactly my week.
screens.why4: It's a card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It is shown on purpose as an idea and reads as a pricing tool that sits on my CRM and CPQ, with nothing slipped in elsewhere or put in words I wouldn't use.
screens.why6: Heard once, it's a long run of five sentences with a colon and two acronyms back to back ('CRM and CPQ'), so I'd hold the gist but lose the benchmarks and leadership lines.
screens.instead: Imagine Veles, one place to build a quote. It works out the price inside your CRM, with deal desk rules and standard terms built in, and shows how comparable deals were priced. The people building it believe it would mean more accurate pricing and less discounting.

screens.why1: Right after an idea about building a quote in one place, asking whether my last deal was already in the CRM makes sense, since I'm always keying deal details into the CRM by hand.
screens.why2: CRM, deal and quote are words I use every day, so I can answer it on first read.
screens.why3: I know whether the opportunity was already in Salesforce when I started my last quote.
screens.why4: A deal is either in the CRM or it isn't, so "Yes, with some steps" is odd here; what I'd actually pick is "Yes, but I had to fill in missing details", and the three wouldn't quite map to that.
screens.why5: The card says plainly what's being imagined, and the question doesn't push the founder's product or terms on me.
screens.why6: It's short and one question, and three short options plus "you can't tell" are easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: Think of your last quote. Was the deal already in your CRM when you started it? Yes, all filled in; Yes, but missing details; No, I had to add it. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the card and the CRM question, asking whether Veles would have helped my last quote is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: The words are plain, but "go better" is loose: I'd have to decide whether it means faster approval, fewer spreadsheets, or a cleaner number, so I'd pause on it.
screens.why3: I just sent a quote and know what slowed it down, so I can judge whether one place to build it would have helped.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it without overlap, and I can't tell fits someone who isn't sure what Veles does yet.
screens.why5: It asks about the quote built in one place, as the card said, and uses no product jargon or role labels I wouldn't use.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is one short balanced question with four short options and the escape at the end, all easy to hold.
screens.instead: Would Veles have got your last quote out and approved faster, or not? A lot faster · A little faster · No difference · Slower · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after asking whether Veles would have helped my last quote, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually move my quoting into it, since that's the real cost of switching for me.
screens.why2: Building quotes in spreadsheets is exactly how I work, so I understand this on first read without any word I wouldn't use.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd give up my Google Sheets pricing workbook and build every quote in a new tool, because I build quotes every week.
screens.why4: The scale is lopsided: there is a conditional yes but no plain 'probably yes', and 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' is so close to what any 'Yes' means that the two blur together.
screens.why5: 'A quote built in one place' instead of spreadsheets keeps the founder's point about quotes scattered across sheets and tools, and it uses no product jargon or role labels I'd stumble on.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four short options I can hold after hearing them once, and the escape is said last as a single phrase.
screens.instead: To use Veles, you'd build every quote in it, not in spreadsheets. Would you do that, or not? Yes; probably yes; probably not; or no. Or say you can't tell.
